questions.q: Define "food" according to the NCERT Class 11 Home Science textbook. Your answer must include the three key processes (ingestion, digestion, assimilation) and the outcome.
questions.a: Food is anything solid or liquid which when swallowed, digested and assimilated in the body provides it with essential substances called nutrients and keeps it well. A wrong answer that omits "assimilated" or says "gives energy only" reveals the student is using a Class 6–7 definition (fuel-only) and has not updated to the senior secondary definition that includes structural, regulatory, and protective roles.

questions.q: A student says, "Nutrition and food mean the same thing — what you eat." Explain why this statement is incorrect using the precise NCERT definitions of both terms.
questions.a: Food is the substance consumed; nutrition is the *science* of foods, nutrients, and their actions within the body (ingestion, digestion, absorption, metabolism, excretion) including social, psychological, and economic dimensions. A wrong answer that equates the two shows the student confuses the *object* (food) with the *process/study* (nutrition) — a classic category error that leads to mistakes in later nodes like RDA interpretation.

questions.q: Classify each of the following as a macronutrient or micronutrient source: (a) wheat roti, (b) spinach, (c) ghee, (d) iodised salt. Justify each classification using the quantity criterion (grams vs milligrams/micrograms per day).
questions.a: (a) Wheat roti → macronutrient source (carbohydrate, required ~130 g/day). (b) Spinach → micronutrient source (iron, folate, vitamin A required in mg/µg/day) though it also provides fibre (macronutrient). (c) Ghee → macronutrient source (fat, required ~25–30 g/day). (d) Iodised salt → micronutrient source (iodine required ~150 µg/day). A wrong answer that calls spinach a "macronutrient food" because "we eat a lot of it" confuses *portion size* with *physiological requirement quantity* — the defining criterion.

questions.q: Compare the energy contribution of 20 g of carbohydrate vs 20 g of fat. Then analyse why the NCERT textbook lists fibre and water under macronutrients even though they provide negligible energy.
questions.a: 20 g carbohydrate = 80 kcal (20 × 4); 20 g fat = 180 kcal (20 × 9). Fibre and water are classified as macronutrients because they are required in *large quantities* (grams per day: fibre ~25–30 g, water ~2–3 L) — the classification is based on *quantity needed*, not energy yield. A wrong answer that says "fibre gives energy" or "water is not a nutrient" reveals the student is using energy-yield as the classification criterion instead of the NCERT's quantity-based criterion.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Since rice provides energy, protein, and B-vitamins, eating only rice in sufficient quantity can meet all nutrient needs." Use the concept of nutrient density and the four functions of food to justify your evaluation.
questions.a: The claim is false. Rice is low in fat (essential fatty acids), vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin B12, calcium, and iron — nutrients critical for regulation (vitamins), protection (antioxidants), and structure (calcium). No single food has high nutrient density for *all* essential nutrients; the "variety" principle in balanced diets exists precisely because nutrient profiles are complementary, not redundant. A wrong answer that agrees reveals the student thinks "energy + some protein + some vitamins = complete nutrition," missing the *qualitative* dimension of nutrient adequacy.

questions.q: Create a one-day meal plan for a Class 11 student that explicitly demonstrates all four functions of food (energy, growth/repair, regulation, protection). Label each food item with its primary function(s) and the nutrient(s) responsible.
questions.a: Example: Breakfast — milk (growth/repair: protein, calcium; energy: lactose, fat), whole wheat toast (energy: carbohydrate; regulation: fibre, B-vitamins), banana (protection: potassium, vitamin B6; energy: carbohydrate). Lunch — dal (growth/repair: protein; regulation: fibre), rice (energy), spinach sabzi (protection: vitamin A, iron, folate; regulation: fibre), curd (growth/repair: protein, calcium; regulation: probiotics). Snack — roasted chana (energy: carb; growth/repair: protein; regulation: fibre). Dinner — fish/chicken or paneer (growth/repair: protein, B12), roti (energy), salad with lemon (protection: vitamin C; regulation: fibre). A poor answer lists foods without linking to specific functions/nutrients, showing the student cannot operationalise the four-role framework.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Food is any solid or liquid substance that, when ingested, digested, and assimilated, provides the body with essential nutrients (______, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre) to supply energy, support growth and repair of tissues, regulate physiological processes, and protect against disease.
Fill in the blank: You feel energised for your morning classes, your muscles recover from ______'s sports practice, and you don't fall sick easily.
What is Food? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Food is any solid or liquid substance that, when ingested, digested, and assimilated, provides the body with essential nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre) to supply energy, support growth and repair of tissues, regulate physiological processes, and protect against disease.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly classify a given food item as a source of macronutrients or micronutrients, explain the four physiological roles of food (energy, growth/repair, regulation, protection) with specific examples, and distinguish between the terms "food," "nutrition," and "nutrients" using precise terminology.
